episode_thesis: Rob Carver argues that systematic portfolios should be judged and sized mainly on Sharpe and robust process, not on drawdown, path risk or recent sector performance: drawdowns carry no information beyond Sharpe and history length, sector leadership in trend following rotates by decade because of single-factor macro stories, and a continuous trend-strength signal already tilts toward whichever asset class is trending. Both speakers hold that true diversification (more commodities, fewer correlated financial markets) is the durable edge, that AI-generated strategy ideas are acceptable only if tested through a process that assumes the idea was conceived with hindsight, and that perpetual futures are a structural change that may hurt hedgers and price discovery.

worldview_premises.premise: Sharpe ratio is the right primary lens for adding, sizing or dropping a strategy; drawdown depth and duration add nothing beyond Sharpe and sample length.
worldview_premises.support: Statistical argument: ignoring autocorrelation drawdown grows with history and shrinks with Sharpe.

worldview_premises.premise: Per-strategy path-risk and loss-clustering analysis overcomplicates and invites overfitting; it is more sensible at whole-portfolio level.
Almost no CTA is a pure trend follower; the trend vs convergent (carry-like) mix is a design choice, constrained for others by client pools and allocator boxes.
worldview_premises.support: Observation of industry practice and his own 40% allocation.

worldview_premises.premise: Skew is a useful label for sorting strategies into trend-like and carry-like buckets, but skew estimates are too statistically unreliable to enter a formal utility function.
worldview_premises.support: Examples: EM FX carry negative skew, developed bond carry mildly positive; robustness argument.

worldview_premises.premise: Hundreds of published factors reduce to a handful of independent drivers, so true diversification is less than the count of factors suggests.
worldview_premises.support: Cites the Alpha Architect piece classifying the factor zoo.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend following in equities is on average net long, so part of its return is the equity risk premium rather than trend skill.
worldview_premises.support: Cites the Beyond Passive Investing post; equities tend to go up.

worldview_premises.premise: Return autocorrelation of trend strategies is too weak to time entry or exit after drawdowns.
worldview_premises.support: His own research and a Winton study; no figures quoted.

worldview_premises.premise: More data is always better; deliberately removing official statistics harms economies and systematic models alike.
Backtest and fitting quality depends more on process than maths, and every idea is formed using future information, whether from AI, data mining or a junior researcher.
worldview_premises.support: Years of research and an upcoming book on backtesting.

decision_process.practice: Continuous trend-strength signals rather than binary; weight scales with trend strength.
decision_process.why: Automatically leans toward trending asset classes without extra sector-timing.

decision_process.practice: About 40% of the portfolio in convergent, non-trend (carry-like) strategies, higher than CTAs who hold 20-30%.
decision_process.why: No client pool or allocator box constraining the mix.

decision_process.practice: Weight a strategy by the probability it works: 10-15% for an outstanding idea, about 0.01% for a weak one, so nothing is ever entirely excluded.
decision_process.why: No idea has zero chance of working.

decision_process.practice: Drop a strategy only on very strong statistical evidence of a structural break; evaluate on Sharpe, not drawdown.
Use skew to classify strategies into buckets and cap the negative-skew bucket (illustrated at 30%), not in a formal utility with Sharpe.
Use AI only for ideas and snippets under 10 lines; test every idea in a process designed for hindsight contamination; ask about research steps, checks and out-of-sample design in due diligence.
decision_process.why: Checking AI code or backtests costs more than writing it.

decision_process.practice: When a pattern appears, ask why it happens first, then whether it is exploitable; test the null.
decision_process.why: Many patterns do not add return and null results are valuable.

decision_process.practice: Rolls futures at expiry (IMM dates); perpetuals would remove roll code.
decision_process.why: Operational convenience, though he views perpetuals as a net negative for markets.

decision_process.practice: Investing into a fund below its high-water mark gets the first returns without performance fees, unless a separate share class has its own high-water mark (host's correction).

disagreements.topic: How to respond to sector rotation in trend following

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Carver endorses diversification yet agrees with tilting the CTA sleeve toward commodities, which is itself a sector weighting call; no rule for how much is stated.

Carver says path risk is not worth analysing per component but later says the Man paper's joint drawdown analysis is a more rigorous crisis-alpha test; the distinction is portfolio level versus component level, not spelled out.
Niels's claim that the 1970s-90s looked like 2000-09 and 2020-26 is conjecture; Carver supplies only the 1970s as supporting data.
The unnamed 'reputable firm' study that commodities are the most consistent crisis sector is not cited or verified.
Neither speaker has read the Beyond Passive Investing paper in detail, and Niels had not read it at all; the neutral-sleeve argument is secondhand.
The Man paper conclusions are described as statistically weak (10-20 drawdown episodes) yet used as a template for a better crisis-alpha test.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) The speakers give no price predictors. Observable inputs they name: a trend barometer (36 = weak conditions), CTA index returns, strength of trend signals by asset class (continuous signal scaling), policy path (Fed chair Warsh hawkish, balance sheet shrinking), oil supply normalisation after the Hormuz deal, and availability of official economic data for macro-trend models. Horizon is months (monthly CTA returns) to decades (sector regimes), with emphasis on robustness over timing.
reader_inferences: (reader) Carver's rejection of drawdown and path-risk metrics implies allocation rules built on Sharpe and probability weights, so a vault feature for 'how this investor sizes a new strategy' should record weight as a function of confidence, not pass/fail.

(reader) The single-factor story for sector dominance (rate cuts then hikes for fixed income, inflation for commodities in the 1970s and 2020s) suggests that sector leadership in trend following depends on macro regime, which links to a regime-detection test rather than performance chasing.
(reader) Niels's incentive argument (assets-based fees favour liquid financials) is a testable proposition for CTA index composition.
(reader) Both speakers treat null results (Quantica) as evidence quality signals, a marker for judging which published claims to weight.
